doc.title: Lisa Parrott interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 22, 2021

title: Australian jazz, Don Burrows and Bernie McGann
summary: Is there an Australian jazz voice? Don Burrows put her on baritone; Bernie McGann is her hero.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: I spoke recently with Adrian Cunningham. And his opinion was that Australia has — I’m trying to remember his exact words but basically he said Australia does not have any indigenous music of its own. How do you feel about that statement?
Well aboriginal people have been playing music for 50,000 years in Australia.

He did mention that, I should have said that, I think that was his exception to what he was thinking. He was talking more about I believe like the pop music and jazz has been fashioned after music from somewhere else.

Yes, yes. I’m a lot older than Adrian, and I was fortunate enough to in the early 80s, I think it was ’83 is when there started to be a jazz course formed at Sydney Conservatorium. So I was there only five years into that program. And Nicki was in the same year also, the bass player I’m going to be playing with on Friday, and his name is Don Burrows. He only recently just passed away, an incredible clarinet, bari, he got me on bari. I owe him everything actually. I owe my career to Don Burrows. He, so this was the year after my tenor got squashed. I was just a soprano player for a year. And he got me playing baritone sax in the big band. He was like, “I think you’d be great on it, you know, I think you have an ear for that, you know. Nicki’s a bass player, you hear that, I think you’d be great on that.” I was like, “I don’t want to carry something like that around.” But he was like, “Just trust me on that, I want to put you in the big band on bari.” Now he is someone who traveled, he was well known over here as well, he traveled all over Europe, he traveled to India and was very, and Brazil, and he took music from all sorts of parts of the world including the States, and formed this jazz course. And at the time the curriculum was very much based around learning standards as a way of learning improvisation. But he was also incredibly encouraging to compose your own music. So those sort of guys, yes I feel like there is an actual thing, there is an Australian quality about Australian jazz. And I feel like I’m a product of that because we’re not as influenced by American jazz so I feel like there’s a lot of Australian jazz musicians who are very unique. Because it’s so isolated. I feel like I came up with my own way of doing things because I was doing gigs from such a young age, before I even went to the Conservatorium. I was already playing gigs because I’d studied classical music and everything and had very good ears and so I was already improvising. So I’d already came up with my own concept of how to do things. And my favorite Australian musicians are like that. And I think isolation breeds that. And case in point, someone like Don Burrows but even more so my hero on the saxophone is Bernie McGann — Bernie McGann – M- C-G-A-N-N. Alto player who just, who just was a total original. I think he was on the scene starting in the late 50s, certainly early 60s. I don’t even know how to describe him. You’d have to — there’s not a lot of recordings because unfortunately the Australian jazz recording industry is definitely — there’s not a lot of recordings of me early in my career

at all either. It was sort of out of our reach financially and just was not available to us. But Bernie McGann, he sounds a bit like Sonny Rollins on alto, some people say he sounds a little bit of Ornette’s sound, that he was already playing that way before he even heard someone like Ornette Coleman. I do feel like Australia has created some quite unique and original sounding musicians who have a different way of, it’s influenced by American jazz but — yeah.
